summary: For ages 5–7, teach that Earth's surface is always changing but at very different speeds: some changes are quick (earthquakes can reshape land in moments, and volcanic eruptions can change it within hours or days) and some are so slow (wind and water wearing rock into sand) that you cannot watch them happen. The core work is contrasting a fast example beside a slow one so the difference in RATE is the focus, sorting events into 'fast' and 'slow', and using before/after evidence to prove slow changes are real changes. Keep everything qualitative — compare fast vs slow, never quantify years (per the NGSS assessment boundary).
misconceptions: 'The Earth never changes / has always looked exactly the same' — the surface is always changing, just often too slowly to see
'Only big dramatic events (eruptions/quakes) are changes' — slow wearing-away by wind and water is change too
'If you can't see it happen, it isn't really happening' — slow changes are real; before/after evidence shows it
'Slow changes are small changes' — given long enough, slow processes carve valleys and wear mountains down
'Fast changes build the land and slow changes only destroy it' — both build and wear down (keep simple: both reshape the land)

activities.title: Same nudge, different world: a shared time control over two scenes
steps: Look at two scenes placed side by side that share ONE time control (for example a slider or scrubber the child drags).
Give the time control the tiniest nudge and watch the left scene: a volcano erupts or an earthquake strikes, reshaping the land very quickly.
Now expect the right scene to change the same way — but notice the cliff barely moves with that same small nudge.
Keep dragging time on and on for the right scene until the cliff slowly wears back and a rough rock gradually rounds into a smooth pebble.
Say out loud which change was fast and which was slow, and agree that BOTH really changed the land.
activities.insight: Some Earth changes are sudden and some are so slow you cannot watch them happen, yet both are real changes to the land. The felt asymmetry — the same action causing wildly different amounts of change — makes the difference in rate experiential rather than just stated.

activities.title: Sort the changes: fast bin or slow bin
steps: Take event cards showing a sudden eruption, a sudden earthquake, gradual cliff wearing-away, gradual pebble smoothing and gradual sand-dune buildup. Use each card’s described conditions and time context, rather than assuming every instance of a process has the same speed.
Place each card into a 'fast' bin or a 'slow' bin.
For at least one card, say why it goes where it goes ('the eruption changed the land quickly, so it's fast').
Answer a 'Which change is slow?' question and a reinforcement question: 'Are the slow changes still real changes to the land?'
activities.insight: In these card examples, the eruption and earthquake are fast changes, and the wearing-away and dune buildup are slow changes. Both kinds genuinely reshape the land. Classifying events can check whether a child compares quick and slow changes.

activities.title: Before and after: proving slow change is real
steps: Look at paired before/after images — for example a cliff that has retreated, or a rough rock that has become a smooth round pebble; alongside a fast pair such as land before and after an eruption.
Tap or point to each spot that is different and name what changed.

Use the source’s time context, such as moments later or a long time later, to tag each pair as fast or slow. If no elapsed-time context is available, state that the images show a change but do not establish its speed.
For the slow pair, answer: 'How do we know this really changed if we never watched it happen?'
activities.insight: Even when we cannot watch a change happen moment to moment, comparing a 'before' and an 'after' is evidence that the change is real. Slow changes leave proof behind.

activities.title: Talk it through: is a wearing-away cliff still changing?
steps: Respond to prompts such as 'Can you think of a fast change to the land? A slow one?'
Explain whether a cliff that is slowly wearing away is still changing, and why.
Give a fresh example of each kind of change in your own words.
Answer the probe: 'If you photographed a cliff today and again a long time from now, would they look the same?'
activities.insight: Putting the idea into your own words — naming examples and defending that a slow, gentle process genuinely changes the land — consolidates and reveals understanding. Recognition in a sort does not by itself show a child can produce and explain examples; this activity targets that production.

checkQuestion: A cliff by the sea slowly wears away as waves hit it, year after year. A volcano can change the land in a single day. Which change is fast and which is slow — and can something as gentle as water really change solid rock?
checkAnswer: The volcano is a fast change (it can reshape the land in a day); the cliff wearing away is a slow change (it takes many years). And yes — even gentle water and wind really do wear away solid rock, but so slowly that we can't watch it happen.
